Every HTML API method used is present in the rendered docs, there were no _doing_it_wrong records, and the implementation follows the documented bookmark, bounded next_token(), depth, seek, set_attribute(), and get_updated_html() pattern.

Correct processor choice and fully documented API usage. It uses the documented direct-child opener checks and clean-scan checks, and passes all cases. Minor idiom miss: the bookmark is not released before returning, although the docs recommend releasing bookmarks when no longer needed.

Correctly uses WP_HTML_Processor with documented structural APIs, bookmarks, depth-bounded token walking, get_last_error()/paused_at_incomplete_token(), set_attribute(), and get_updated_html(). No undocumented methods or misuse records.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 11 hidden cases, so there were no failed hidden cases to attribute to a misconception. The docs did well in three important places: the processor-choice guidance clearly points structure-sensitive work to WP_HTML_Processor; the 'scan a region before editing its opener' recipe gives the exact bookmark/seek/update shape; and the 'test subtree membership and direct children' plus get_current_depth() text explains why direct child openers require #tag, !is_tag_closer(), and depth == container_depth + 1. Those passages prevented over-counting nested LI elements and handled omitted LI closers. The incomplete and unsupported cases were also handled because the docs tell callers to check paused_at_incomplete_token() and get_last_error() after the bounded scan before mutating. Near-misses: trial-2 omitted release_bookmark(), and the rendered next_token() method section still contains a confusing 'do not use' since-note despite the overview recipes relying on it as public guidance.

doc_gaps.problem: The method body and overview recipes present next_token() as the right public tool for subtree walks, but the Since note still says 'Added for internal support; do not use.'
doc_gaps.suggestion: Remove or revise the stale 'do not use' language so it matches the documented public recipes for token walking with structural awareness.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor::get_last_error(), paused_at_incomplete_token(), and HTML Support wording
doc_gaps.problem: The docs say unsupported markup in the input aborts processing, but do not make the cursor-local timing fully explicit. A reader can infer that later unsupported or incomplete syntax invalidates an already-completed bounded subtree scan.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that these indicators report what the processor has encountered so far. Add a general note that a bounded subtree walk can validate the scanned region without proving the rest of the document tail is complete.

doc_gaps.problem: The method-level bookmark example is inherited-style Tag Processor code, while structure-aware bookmark use requires WP_HTML_Processor patterns and explicit cleanup.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add an HTML Processor-specific bookmark example that records an opener, walks descendants by depth, seeks back to mutate the opener, and releases the bookmark on success and fallback paths.

The extra class-existence guard is unnecessary in this environment, and the solution missed the direct `normalize()` API, but the chosen serialization path is documented and behaviorally sound.

verdict.failure_analysis:
All trials passed all seven hidden cases. The rendered docs did well on the core decisions: the HTML Processor overview says to choose `WP_HTML_Processor` for normalizing markup; the support section says unsupported markup makes `serialize()` and `normalize()` return `null`; the `normalize()` and `serialize()` sections both document attribute quoting, omitted-tag insertion, table normalization, entity preservation/re-encoding, and omission of incomplete trailing syntax. That was enough for every candidate to avoid the Tag Processor and avoid hand-rolled serialization.

The main near-miss is discoverability rather than correctness. All three candidates implemented `create_fragment($html)->serialize()` instead of `WP_HTML_Processor::normalize($html)`, even though the task was exactly a body-fragment normalization task. This suggests the Usage section's general three-step pattern is more salient than the later static `normalize()` method section. The docs describe the direct method correctly, but they do not make it the obvious first choice for the common case: “I have a body fragment and want normalized HTML or null.”

A second near-miss is failure signaling. The docs state output methods return `null` on unsupported markup, but the execution records also captured `WP_HTML_Processor::serialize` warnings for unsupported parser errors. The candidates still behaved correctly because tests measured returned strings, but callers using warning-sensitive harnesses may be surprised unless the docs distinguish return-value failure policy from emitted warnings.

doc_gaps.problem: The primary usage recipe emphasizes creating a processor, finding a location, and requesting changes. For pure body-fragment normalization, that flow hides the simpler static API.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short “Normalize a BODY fragment” recipe before the general traversal/editing steps: prefer `WP_HTML_Processor::normalize( $html )` when no custom context, full-document mode, or token inspection is needed; handle `null` according to the caller's failure policy.

doc_gaps.problem: The method documents behavior and examples, but does not explicitly position itself as the preferred convenience wrapper for default body-context fragment normalization.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add one sentence to the contract: this is equivalent to creating a default BODY fragment processor and serializing it, and should be preferred for one-shot normalization of ordinary fragments.

doc_gaps.problem: Docs say `serialize()` and `normalize()` return `null` when unable to produce output, but do not mention that serialization may also emit a warning when the parser has an unsupported-markup error.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document the observable failure mode: callers should treat `null` as the programmatic failure signal, and serialization of unsupported markup may emit a warning through WordPress error handling.

trials.notes: Used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), one next_token() walk, get_token_type(), get_token_name(), is_tag_closer(), get_current_depth(), and get_modifiable_text(), all documented. It follows the docs' one-cursor state-machine guidance, limits text collection to #text tokens, handles decoded entity text, null processor creation, empty headings, and virtual/implied closers.

Used only documented APIs and chose the HTML Processor correctly. The depth-bounded subtree walk with get_current_depth() >= opener depth is exactly the documented text-extraction pattern. Minor idiom deduction because the docs advise preferring a single next_token() loop for repeated regions, while this uses an outer next_tag() loop with an inner next_token() loop; it is bounded correctly and passes here. The is_tag_closer() guard after plain next_tag() is redundant because closers are skipped by default.

Used only documented APIs and the correct processor. It uses a single next_token() state machine and collects only #text via get_modifiable_text(), so decoded text and inline markup are handled correctly. Minor deduction because it relies on heading closer tokens instead of recording a subtree depth/breadcrumb boundary, and adds an unnecessary class_exists() environment guard, but the closer-driven approach is supported by the docs' statement that next_token() visits implicit and end-of-input closers.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 7 frozen cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to a documentation gap. The docs worked well for this task because they explicitly direct structure-sensitive text extraction to WP_HTML_Processor rather than WP_HTML_Tag_Processor, document create_fragment() for BODY fragments, and include a close recipe under "collect DOM-style text from a subtree": record opener depth, walk with next_token(), append only #text tokens, and read decoded text with get_modifiable_text(). The get_current_depth() section also explains the >= boundary and virtual/implied closer behavior, which likely prevented failures on nested inline markup, entity decoding, empty headings, uppercase source tags, and omitted closing tags. Near-misses were mostly stylistic: one trial used nested cursor walks despite the warning to prefer one next_token() loop for repeated regions, and another relied on closer tokens rather than depth. Both choices are defensible from the current docs, but the nested-loop warning is broad enough that a subject could be unsure whether a bounded subtree scan inside an outer search is acceptable.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn against nested next_token() loops for repeated regions, but nearby examples and the canonical pattern still use a bounded inner subtree walk after next_tag(). This leaves ambiguity about when nested scanning is actually unsafe versus merely less preferred.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify the contract with a short rule: nested subtree walks are acceptable when the caller intentionally consumes the region boundary and resumes after it; use a single state-machine loop when the outer loop still needs to observe every boundary token or sibling opener.

doc_gaps.problem: Both methods can identify tag names during token walks, but the practical distinction is scattered. Trial code used both styles successfully, suggesting the docs are sufficient but could be easier to apply.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a concise comparison note: use get_tag() when matched on tags; use get_token_name() when a token-walking state machine wants DOM-like names, and guard with get_token_type() === '#tag' before interpreting dynamic names as element names.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs mention paused_at_incomplete_token() and get_last_error(), but subjects did not discuss a deliberate best-effort versus all-or-nothing policy. For read-only extraction this was fine, but callers may miss that this is a caller contract decision.
doc_gaps.suggestion: End the subtree text recipe with two labeled policy snippets: best-effort extraction returns accumulated text after the walk, while complete-input extraction rejects or falls back when paused_at_incomplete_token() or get_last_error() indicates an incomplete or unsupported parse.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial. Near-miss: the add_class() method section documents class-list semantics clearly, but the exact placement/serialization of a newly created class attribute is easier to infer from broader attribute-update docs than from add_class() itself.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden cases failed across the three trials. The rendered docs supported the solution well: the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use it for flat tag/name/class attribute edits and byte-precise preservation; the Usage and Finding tags sections show construction with new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor($html) and next_tag(); the get_attribute section distinguishes null for absent, empty string for present-empty, and true for valueless boolean attributes; set_attribute documents overwriting existing attributes and where newly added attributes are inserted; get_updated_html documents that untouched bytes are returned exactly. verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three candidates passed all 8 frozen expectations. The docs worked well because the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use WP_HTML_Processor for collecting element text and walking subtrees, while the HTML Processor's "Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree" directly demonstrates the needed pattern: create a fragment parser, find a container tag, record current depth, walk with next_token(), append only #text tokens, and call get_modifiable_text(). The next_token(), get_current_depth(), and get_modifiable_text() sections also cover the key edge cases: text may be split across tokens, token walks do not stop automatically at an element boundary, get_modifiable_text() is already decoded for #text nodes, unguarded modifiable text is too broad, and read-only extraction may choose its own policy for incomplete input. The only near-miss was that trials 1 and 2 added an unnecessary is_tag_closer() check after next_tag('H1'), suggesting the default opener-only behavior of next_tag() was understood well enough to pass but not fully internalized.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs state in the parameter table that tag closers are skipped by default, but examples elsewhere still include is_tag_closer() checks. This can leave readers unsure whether next_tag('TAG') can return a closer.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short prose note near the simple string-query examples: plain next_tag('TAG') matches opening tags only; use tag_closers => 'visit' before is_tag_closer() matters.

doc_gaps.problem: The depth-bounded walk contract is documented, but the related guarantees for empty elements, virtual/end-of-input closers, and read-only incomplete-input policy are spread across multiple sections.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Consolidate a compact contract note for subtree scans: record opener depth, continue while depth >= opener depth, append desired token types, the first shallower token is outside the subtree, empty subtrees yield no text tokens, and callers decide whether paused_at_incomplete_token() matters.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden cases failed across the three trials; all passed 7/7 with no _doing_it_wrong records. The docs did well in the WP_HTML_Tag_Processor 'Building markup from a template' section: it directly teaches the successful pattern of starting from a literal template, predeclaring attributes to preserve order, including placeholder text, using set_attribute() for plain unescaped attribute values, using set_modifiable_text() for plain unescaped text, and returning get_updated_html(). The set_attribute() section also clearly explains automatic encoding and attribute placement, which prevented failures in quotes-in-alt and special-chars-in-url. The set_modifiable_text() section clearly says empty elements have no text token and includes a placeholder-text example, which prevented caption insertion failures for ampersands, angle brackets, and script-looking text. Near misses: trials 2 and 3 chose the HTML Processor, likely because the processor-choice docs say to use it when structure/text collection matters and because create_fragment() sounds natural for building fragments. Also, all trials ignored the documented instruction to check set_modifiable_text()'s return value, probably because the examples themselves do not check it.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Tag_Processor overview, 'Which processor should I use?' and 'Building markup from a template'
doc_gaps.problem: The processor-choice guidance does not explicitly say that filling a known markup template with attributes and placeholder text is still a Tag Processor use case, even when the template has nested elements.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a decision-table row: 'Known template / fill attributes / replace placeholder text -> WP_HTML_Tag_Processor; unknown document structure, subtree text extraction, implied tags, or normalized serialization -> WP_HTML_Processor.'

doc_gaps.problem: The page says HTML Processor builds on Tag Processor, but inherited mutation methods such as set_modifiable_text() and get_updated_html() are not consistently surfaced in the method index. This makes valid inherited calls look semi-undocumented.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add an 'Inherited mutation APIs from WP_HTML_Tag_Processor' subsection listing set_attribute(), set_modifiable_text(), remove_attribute(), add_class(), remove_class(), and get_updated_html(), with a short note that serialize()/serialize_token() are for normalization/rewrite, not queued edits.

doc_gaps.problem: The rendered docs still contain the stale sentence 'The Tag Processor currently only supports the tag token,' while other sections and examples rely on #text tokens.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Replace that sentence with current behavior: next_token() can visit tags, text, comments, doctypes, and related syntax tokens; callers should use get_token_type() to select #text before reading or writing text.

doc_gaps.problem: The prose says 'Always check the return value,' but the nearby examples call set_modifiable_text() without checking it. The trials copied the unchecked style.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 10 hidden cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs did well on the exact hard parts of this task: the HTML Processor overview says to choose WP_HTML_Processor when structure matters and when collecting element text; create_fragment() is documented as the BODY-fragment factory; next_token() explains that text can be split across multiple #text tokens and that SCRIPT/STYLE/TITLE/TEXTAREA carry no #text children; get_modifiable_text() clearly says #text, TITLE, and TEXTAREA are decoded UTF-8, while SCRIPT/STYLE are raw; and the text-extraction recipe warns not to treat every token with modifiable text as ordinary DOM text. Near-misses were small: trials 2 and 3 leaned on get_token_name()/is_tag_closer() behavior for non-tag tokens instead of first checking #tag, and none checked paused_at_incomplete_token() or get_last_error(); however the docs explicitly leave read-only incomplete-input policy to the caller, and the task did not require rejecting partial scans.

doc_gaps.problem: The examples show tag-only use, but the return contract for non-tag tokens is implicit. Trial code safely relied on false for non-tags, but a reader has to infer that from implementation or from broader token docs.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add one sentence: when not matched on a tag token, this method returns false; callers that need an opening element should prefer get_token_type() === '#tag' && ! is_tag_closer().

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain ordinary subtree text and named special-element text separately. This task required a combined policy: all ordinary body text plus selected decoded special elements, excluding raw special elements. The subjects inferred it correctly, but the distinction is subtle.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short general example or policy note showing how to combine ordinary #text collection with an explicit whitelist of decoded special-element opener text, while leaving SCRIPT/STYLE raw text out unless specifically requested.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 8 hidden cases, with no _doing_it_wrong or trigger_error records. The docs succeeded on the key concepts: the processor-selection guidance points structural text extraction to WP_HTML_Processor; get_attribute documents string|true|null and decoded values, which led all trials to exclude missing/valueless hrefs and avoid double-decoding; next_token/get_current_depth explain subtree walking and virtual closers, which covered the unclosed-link case; and get_modifiable_text warns to read ordinary DOM-style text only from #text tokens, which avoided including markup, comments, or img alt text. verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in this round: all three trials passed 8/8 with no _doing_it_wrong records. The docs did the important work well: the 'Which processor should I use?' guidance points structural text extraction toward WP_HTML_Processor; create_fragment() clearly fits body fragments; next_token() explains implied/virtual closers, synthesized table structure, one shared cursor, and depth-bounded walks; get_modifiable_text() clearly states decoded #text semantics and warns not to treat all modifiable text as DOM text. The near misses were not hidden-test failures: trial-1 did not use its recorded table depth to bound the table, relying instead on a TABLE closer; trial-3 skipped structurally empty rows because it guarded the row flush with empty(); and none of the trials made an explicit all-or-nothing choice using paused_at_incomplete_token() or get_last_error(), though the task and reference accepted best-effort read-only extraction.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 8 hidden cases. The docs did well in the exact areas this task needed: the Tag Processor overview says to use the HTML Processor for missing closing tags and normalized output; the HTML Processor text-extraction recipe says ordinary text means #text tokens only, not every token with modifiable text; get_modifiable_text() states #text/TITLE/TEXTAREA text is decoded while comments/raw-text sections differ; and serialize_token() explicitly documents token-by-token normalized rewrites, including wrapping selected text tokens. These passages explain why the candidates avoided matching attributes/comments, matched entity-encoded keywords, preserved split text-node behavior, and produced normalized implied closers. The main near-miss is the shared fallback explanation: all candidates call normalize($html) after a rewrite loop if get_last_error() is non-null. The docs do warn that normalize($html) starts over from the original bytes and discards emitted changes, so this is not a hallucination, but it is a contract risk for unsupported markup after earlier matches. They also did not check paused_at_incomplete_token(); for this normalized-output task the accumulated serialization omits unvisited incomplete trailing syntax, which is acceptable, but tasks requiring complete source bytes would need that check.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that normalize($html) discards emitted rewrite output, but the candidates still treated normalize($html) ?? $html as a generic recovery path after a rewrite loop.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short decision table for rewrite-loop failure policy: strict contract returns null/empty or throws; best-effort returns accumulated output; fallback normalization deliberately discards all emitted rewrites; raw input fallback is not normalized output.

doc_gaps.problem: The relationship between processor-creation failure, unsupported-markup aborts, and normalized-output contracts is spread across multiple sections.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Cross-link the factory and normalization docs to the rewrite-loop policy, explicitly stating that normalize($html) is only a fresh normalization of original input, not recovery of a partially serialized transformation.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain that SCRIPT/STYLE/TITLE/TEXTAREA carry text on opener tokens, but this remains easy to miss when a task says ordinary text nodes only.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a small token-stream example for ordinary text versus special-element opener text, showing that callers should require get_token_type() === '#text' unless they explicitly opt into those element contents.

Essentially matches the canonical documented pattern: Tag Processor, single forward scan, repeated same-name bookmark, seek, add_class(), get_updated_html(). Not releasing the bookmark is harmless because the processor immediately goes out of scope. No undocumented HTML API usage.

All HTML API methods used are documented, and the implementation passes. The main adherence issue is processor choice: it uses WP_HTML_Processor, tries create_full_parser() before create_fragment(), and feature-probes methods, despite the docs recommending WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat position-based class edits. It also does not check get_last_error() after using the HTML Processor, so unsupported markup could make the 'last H2' scan untrustworthy outside the tested cases.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all hidden cases. The docs did well on the core concepts: the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use it for flat tag/name/class edits; next_tag() documents string tag queries, case-insensitive tag matching, opener-only default behavior, and that tag-like text inside comments is not matched; set_bookmark() explicitly teaches the 'remember the last matching tag by re-setting the same bookmark name, then seek once' idiom; add_class() explains missing and existing class behavior; get_updated_html() explains how to read back queued mutations while preserving untouched bytes. The near-miss was trial-3: it still worked because WP_HTML_Processor inherits the mutation APIs, but it treated the full parser as a generic first choice and skipped the HTML Processor's abort/error checks. That suggests the processor-selection guidance is present but not quite strong enough at the exact factory/API decision point.

doc_gaps.problem: A reader can still treat create_full_parser() as a generic preferred constructor and create_fragment() as a fallback, as trial-3 did.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a compact factory-selection table: use create_fragment() for BODY fragments, create_full_parser() only for complete documents, and use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor directly for flat class/attribute edits that do not need tree structure.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say the HTML Processor aborts on unsupported markup, but the consequence for deferred mutations after a scan is easy to miss.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance that if a scan result determines a later mutation, callers using WP_HTML_Processor should check get_last_error() after the scan before trusting 'none found' or 'last found'; otherwise prefer WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for lexical tag edits.

doc_gaps.problem: The last-match bookmark idiom is documented well in set_bookmark(), but it is buried in a long method section and illustrated with nested list logic.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short general recipe near the Bookmarks overview for 'update the last matching tag in one pass' using a neutral example such as the last matching link or image, showing repeated set_bookmark(), seek(), mutation, and get_updated_html().

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed across the three trials. The docs did well on the key decisions: the Tag Processor overview says it is the right choice for flat attribute/class edits with byte-precise preservation; the Usage section shows direct construction with `new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor( $html )` and `next_tag()` walking; `get_attribute_names_with_prefix()` documents lowercase returned names and case-insensitive matching; `next_tag()` documents that comments/raw-text are not matched as tags and incomplete trailing tags are not modified; `get_updated_html()` clearly states it is the output method after queued mutations. Near-misses: the prefix helper’s `null` contract is documented, but the matched-tag/no-matches case is not explicitly shown as `array()`, so subjects had to infer that `null` only means “not on a tag opener.” Also, exact prefix boundary behavior is semantically implied by “prefix,” but no example contrasts `data-track-` with similar names like `data-track` or `data-tracker`.

doc_gaps.problem: Return semantics are underspecified for a matched tag with no matching attributes. The docs say `array|null` and `null when no tag opener is matched`, but only demonstrate matches and the post-scan `null` case.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short example showing three states: before/after no matched opener returns `null`, matched opener with no prefix matches returns `array()`, and matched opener with case-variant matches returns lowercase names.

doc_gaps.problem: The case-insensitive behavior is documented, but exact prefix boundary behavior is not illustrated. This matters when similar attribute names differ only by a hyphen or suffix.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general example showing that prefix matching is literal after ASCII case folding: a prefix like `data-foo-` matches `DATA-FOO-ID` but not `data-foo` or `data-foobar`.

doc_gaps.problem: The detailed method section is terse and only says whether an attribute was removed. The safer no-op contract for absent attributes appears earlier in the overview, so readers landing on the method may miss it.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Repeat the contract in the method docblock: removing an absent attribute is safe and has no effect, matching is case-insensitive for HTML attributes, and callers normally do not need to branch on the boolean before calling `get_updated_html()`.

The main API-pattern failure is semantic: it used a skip-depth subtree deletion pattern, so it removed SPAN contents instead of only omitting the SPAN opener/closer tokens. That contradicts the documented serialize_token() wrapper-removal example.

verdict.failure_analysis: Trial 2 failed simple, nested-spans, attributes-discarded, adjacent-spans, span-with-block-content, and unclosed-span for the same misconception: it treated "remove the SPAN element" as "remove the SPAN subtree." The code increments $skip_depth on a SPAN opener and suppresses every descendant token until the SPAN closer, so text, child elements, adjacent span text, block/void content, and text inside an unclosed SPAN are all dropped. The responsible documentation area is WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token(), especially the rewrite guidance and its example "Remove every SUP element but keep its contents," which shows the correct general pattern: skip matching tag tokens and serialize everything else. The docs were strong enough for trials 1 and 3, but trial 2 shows that the phrase "skip tokens to remove them" can still be overgeneralized into a subtree-skip algorithm. For unclosed-span specifically, next_token() correctly emits a virtual SPAN closer at end of input; the docs describe that closers are visited for unclosed elements, but they do not explicitly warn that a stateful subtree skip will remain active through all trailing content until that virtual closer.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token() docblock and "Recipe: rewrite while serializing tokens"
doc_gaps.problem: The docs show an unwrap-style example, but they do not explicitly contrast wrapper removal with subtree deletion. A reader can infer that tracking depth and skipping while inside the element is the safer way to "remove" an element.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short distinction: to unwrap/remove only an element's own tags, skip matching opener and closer tokens and serialize descendants; to delete an element and all descendants, record depth at the opener and skip until leaving that subtree. Call out that a skip-depth counter deletes contents.

doc_gaps.problem: It is not emphasized that during a token walk, get_tag() matches both opener and closer tag tokens, while text and descendant tokens have no matching tag name.
doc_gaps.suggestion: In token-rewrite examples, state that `if ( 'X' === $processor->get_tag() ) continue;` skips both wrapper tag tokens and preserves all non-X descendant tokens.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs describe virtual closers for unclosed elements, but not their practical effect on rewrite state machines.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a note that subtree-skip state remains active until parser-reported closers, including virtual end-of-input closers; wrapper-unwrapping filters should skip only the element tag tokens when trailing content must remain.

doc_gaps.problem: Near misses used raw input or normalize($html) as fallbacks. Those policies are documented, but it is easy to miss that they discard token-loop rewrites and may violate contracts requiring modified normalized output.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify in fallback guidance that raw input and normalize($html) intentionally discard emitted changes; examples for string-returning rewriters should name which fallback preserves the function's contract and which does not.
